description: Sensory, relay and motor neurons, synaptic transmission, excitation, inhibition and Hebb.
content_html:
Types of Neuron

The nervous system works because of specialised cells called neurons. There are three main types, each with a different role in passing information around the body. Psychologists study neurons because understanding how signals travel between them helps explain how we learn, react and behave.

Sensory neurons carry information from the body’s sense organs — the eyes, ears, nose, skin and taste receptors — to the central nervous system. When you touch a hot surface, sensory neurons fire a signal towards the spinal cord and brain before you are even consciously aware of the danger.

Relay neurons act as connectors within the CNS. They receive signals from sensory neurons, process them, and pass them on to motor neurons or other relay neurons. Most of the neurons in the brain are relay neurons, making them central to thinking, memory and decision-making.

Motor neurons carry instructions from the CNS to the muscles and glands. When you decide to move your hand away from the heat, motor neurons carry that instruction from your spinal cord to the muscles in your arm, triggering contraction.

Key Fact

Three neuron types: sensory (sense organs → CNS), relay (connects within CNS), motor (CNS → muscles/glands). The typical sequence when you respond to a stimulus is sensory → relay → motor.

Synaptic Transmission

Neurons do not touch each other. The tiny gap between them is called a synapse. When an electrical signal (called an action potential) reaches the end of a neuron, it triggers the release of neurotransmitters — chemical messengers stored in small packages called vesicles at the end of the sending (pre-synaptic) neuron.

The neurotransmitters drift across the synapse and bind to receptor sites on the receiving (post-synaptic) neuron. This binding either starts a new electrical signal in the receiving neuron or prevents one from firing. Once the signal is passed, the neurotransmitters are either broken down or drawn back into the pre-synaptic neuron in a process called reuptake.

When a neurotransmitter binds to the post-synaptic neuron and makes it more likely to fire an action potential, this is called excitation. Excitatory neurotransmitters “turn up the volume” on neural activity.

When binding makes the receiving neuron less likely to fire, this is called inhibition. Inhibitory neurotransmitters act as “brakes,” preventing unwanted signals from spreading. The nervous system depends on a balance between excitation and inhibition — too much excitation can cause a seizure; too much inhibition can slow responses dangerously.

Neurotransmitters and Behaviour

Different neurotransmitters have different effects depending on which neurons they act upon. Dopamine is involved in the brain’s reward system — it is released during pleasurable experiences and reward-seeking behaviour, reinforcing the actions that led to the reward. This mechanism also underlies addiction. Serotonin contributes to feelings of well-being and emotional stability. These neurotransmitters are relevant to psychology because many mental health conditions — including depression and anxiety — are associated with imbalances in neurotransmitter levels, and many psychiatric medications work by altering the availability of neurotransmitters at the synapse.

For example, a class of antidepressants known as SSRIs (Selective Serotonin Reuptake Inhibitors) works by blocking the reuptake of serotonin. Because serotonin is not drawn back into the pre-synaptic neuron as quickly, it remains in the synapse for longer and continues to stimulate the post-synaptic receptor. This illustrates how a change at the synapse level can have wide-reaching effects on mood and behaviour — demonstrating the direct link between neurochemistry and psychological experience.

Hebb’s Theory of Learning and Neuronal Growth

In 1949, the psychologist Donald Hebb proposed that learning changes the connections between neurons. His core idea is often summarised as: “neurons that fire together, wire together.” This is known as Hebbian learning.

According to Hebb, every time two neurons fire together, the synapse between them is strengthened — the pre-synaptic neuron becomes better at triggering the post-synaptic one. Over repeated activation, new synaptic connections form and existing ones grow stronger. This process, known as synaptic plasticity, is the biological basis of learning and memory. A practical example is learning a musical instrument: initially, playing a scale requires conscious effort as the relevant neural pathways are weak. With practice, the pathways strengthen and the movement becomes fluent and automatic — Hebb’s mechanism in action.

Key Fact

Hebb (1949): when neurons fire repeatedly together, the synapse between them strengthens. This “neurons that fire together, wire together” principle explains how practice and repetition create durable memories and skills.

A strength of Hebb’s theory is that it is supported by later research. The discovery of long-term potentiation (LTP) — a process by which repeated neural activity strengthens synaptic connections — provides direct physiological evidence for Hebb’s mechanism. Brain scanning research confirms that practising a skill increases neural connectivity in the relevant areas.

A weakness is that Hebb’s theory was proposed before the technology to observe synapses in living brains existed, so it was initially theoretical. Additionally, the theory focuses on a “bottom-up” strengthening of connections but does not fully explain how we deliberately choose what to learn or how some memories are forgotten despite repeated practice.
exam_tip_html: When describing synaptic transmission, work through the sequence: action potential arrives → neurotransmitters released into synapse → bind to post-synaptic receptors → excitation or inhibition → reuptake. Examiners expect you to use these specific terms. For Hebb’s theory, state the year (1949), the mechanism (repeated co-activation strengthens the synapse) and the phrase “neurons that fire together, wire together” — but don’t treat the phrase as the full answer; explain the mechanism behind it.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Three neuron types carry information: sensory (sense organs to CNS), relay (within CNS), motor (CNS to muscles/glands). The typical response sequence is sensory → relay → motor.
  • Synaptic transmission involves neurotransmitters crossing the synapse and binding to post-synaptic receptors, causing either excitation (increased firing likelihood) or inhibition (decreased firing likelihood), followed by reuptake.
  • Hebb’s theory (1949) proposes that repeated co-firing of neurons strengthens the synapse between them — the biological basis of learning and memory.

practice_questions.text:
Which type of neuron carries information from the sense organs to the central nervous system?
A) Motor neuron
B) Relay neuron
C) Sensory neuron
D) Efferent neuron

practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A precise definition identifying it as the tiny gap between two neurons across which neurotransmitters (chemical messengers) pass — both elements stated [2 marks].
Secure: Correct core idea — a gap between neurons — without reference to chemical transmission [1 mark].
Developing: Vague reference to a space or connection between cells [0–1 mark].
Emerging: Incorrect or irrelevant [0 marks].

practice_questions.text: Describe the process of synaptic transmission.
practice_questions.marks:
Award 1 mark per accurate step up to 3 marks. Students may include: an action potential reaches the pre-synaptic neuron; neurotransmitters are released from vesicles into the synapse; neurotransmitters bind to receptor sites on the post-synaptic neuron; this causes excitation or inhibition; neurotransmitters are broken down or taken back up via reuptake.
Mastering: Three clear sequential steps using accurate terminology.
Secure: Three steps identified but some terms imprecise.
Developing: Two steps described.
Emerging: One step or a vague description of chemicals crossing a gap.

practice_questions.text: Explain the difference between excitation and inhibition in synaptic transmission.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Clear distinction between excitation (increases likelihood of post-synaptic neuron firing) and inhibition (decreases likelihood), with an explanation of why the balance between them matters for normal brain function. Two developed points.
Secure: Both concepts correctly defined with some explanation of their effects.
Developing: One concept correctly described or both partially described.
Emerging: Vague reference to signals being “sent” or “blocked” without using correct terms.

practice_questions.text: Describe Hebb's theory of learning and neuronal growth, including the aim, the key idea and the evidence that supports it.
practice_questions.marks:
Award marks for: Hebb proposed the theory in 1949 (1); the theory states that repeated co-firing of two neurons strengthens the synapse between them (1); often summarised as 'neurons that fire together, wire together' (1); this means that practice and repetition physically change the brain by creating stronger neural connections (1); later research into long-term potentiation (LTP) supports this mechanism (1).
Mastering: All five points included with clear explanation of the mechanism.
Secure: Four points included.
Developing: Two or three points.
Emerging: Vague reference to learning changing the brain without specifying the mechanism.

practice_questions.text: Describe and evaluate Hebb's theory of learning and neuronal growth.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Accurate description of the theory (year, mechanism, 'fire together wire together'), how it explains skill-learning and memory through synaptic strengthening; two elaborated evaluation points (e.g. supported by LTP research as a strength; doesn't explain forgetting or intentional learning as a weakness), each developed with a reason.
Secure: Accurate description; two evaluation points with some development.
Developing: Partially correct description; one elaborated evaluation point or two undeveloped ones.
Emerging: Basic description; evaluation is a single unsupported claim.
[AO1 description ~4 marks; AO3 evaluation ~5 marks]

knowledge_checks.q: What is the role of motor neurons in the nervous system?
options: Carry sensory information from the skin to the CNS
Connect sensory neurons to other neurons within the CNS
Carry instructions from the CNS to muscles and glands

knowledge_checks.q: According to Hebb's theory, what happens to the synapse between two neurons when they fire together repeatedly?
options: It becomes weaker and eventually disappears
It strengthens, making future co-firing more likely

knowledge_checks.q: Neurotransmitters are stored in small packages called _____ at the end of the pre-synaptic neuron.
When a neurotransmitter makes the post-synaptic neuron less likely to fire, this is called _____.
Match each neuron type to its function.
right: Carries signals from sense organs to the CNS
Carries instructions from the CNS to muscles

flashcard_questions.q: What does a sensory neuron carry and in which direction?
flashcard_questions.a: Information from sense organs to the central nervous system.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the role of relay neurons in the nervous system?
flashcard_questions.a: Connect sensory and motor neurons within the CNS, processing information.

flashcard_questions.q: What does a motor neuron carry and where does it deliver it?
flashcard_questions.a: Instructions from the CNS to muscles or glands.
The tiny gap between two neurons across which neurotransmitters pass.

flashcard_questions.q: What triggers the release of neurotransmitters into the synapse?
flashcard_questions.a: An action potential (electrical signal) arriving at the pre-synaptic neuron.

flashcard_questions.q: What is reuptake in synaptic transmission?
flashcard_questions.a: Neurotransmitters being absorbed back into the pre-synaptic neuron after use.

flashcard_questions.q: What does excitation mean in the context of synaptic transmission?
flashcard_questions.a: A neurotransmitter makes the post-synaptic neuron more likely to fire.

flashcard_questions.q: What does inhibition mean in the context of synaptic transmission?
flashcard_questions.a: A neurotransmitter makes the post-synaptic neuron less likely to fire.

flashcard_questions.q: Hebb (1949) proposed that learning occurs when neurons that _____ together, _____ together.
What year did Hebb propose his theory of learning and neuronal growth?
What physical change does Hebb's theory say repeated co-firing produces at the synapse?
flashcard_questions.a: The synapse strengthens, making future co-firing more likely.

flashcard_questions.q: What later discovery supports Hebb's theory?
flashcard_questions.a: Long-term potentiation (LTP) — repeated neural activity strengthens synaptic connections.

glossary_terms.definition: A specialised nerve cell that processes and transmits information through electrical and chemical signals.
Neurons that carry sensory information from sense organs (eyes, ears, skin) to the central nervous system.
Neurons found mainly in the brain and spinal cord that connect sensory neurons to motor neurons, processing and integrating information.
Neurons that carry instructions from the CNS to muscles or glands, triggering movement or secretion.
The tiny gap between two neurons across which chemical messages (neurotransmitters) pass.
Chemical messengers released into a synapse that carry signals from one neuron to the next.
The process by which neurotransmitters are absorbed back into the pre-synaptic neuron after crossing the synapse, ready to be used again.
The effect of a neurotransmitter that increases the likelihood that the receiving neuron will fire an action potential.
The effect of a neurotransmitter that decreases the likelihood that the receiving neuron will fire an action potential.
Hebb's proposal that when two neurons repeatedly fire at the same time, the synapse between them becomes stronger, making future firing more likely.
A neurotransmitter that plays a key role in mood, reward and motivation; low levels are associated with depression.
A neurotransmitter that contributes to feelings of well-being and happiness; also involved in sleep and appetite regulation.
